scenes.title: Where and when
narration: The loure originated in Normandy, France, named after a local bagpipe called the loure.
It emerged as a theatrical dance in the late 17th and early 18th centuries, closely linked to French Baroque music and dance traditions.

It was introduced by composers like Lully and popularized by Rameau and Bach, evolving from a folk dance to a slow, ceremonious stage dance characterized by a dotted rhythm and emphasis on the first beat.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: The loure was primarily a theatrical dance performed in ballets and operas of the late 17th and early 18th centuries.
It conveyed noble, majestic, and pastoral moods, often associated with ceremonial or courtly occasions.
It was not a social ballroom dance but a virtuosic stage performance.
Today it is a living tradition.

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: The loure is danced slowly or at a moderate tempo, often in compound duple meter (6/4) or simple triple meter (3/4).
It features two steps per measure with complex sequences and continuous ornamentation.
The first beat is strongly accented, preceded by an anacrusis.
Watch for Loure step, Elegant turn.

scenes.title: Listen
narration: The loure's music is characterized by a lilting dotted rhythm, often with an anacrusis of an eighth and a quarter note.
It is usually in compound duple or simple triple meter, with a slow or moderate tempo.
Listen for the Baroque strings, woodwinds, musette (bagpipe).
The pulse is compound duple (6/4) or simple triple (3/4).

The loure features a slow, lilting dotted rhythm with a strong downbeat preceded by a pickup note, creating a majestic and ceremonious sound. The music often includes contrapuntal textures and dynamic contrasts, with Baroque strings and woodwinds enriched by the musette's drone-like timbre.

scenes.title: The people
narration: Key figures associated with the loure include Jean-Baptiste Lully, who introduced it in stage works like Alceste; Jean-Philippe Rameau, who composed numerous loures with imaginative orchestration; Johann Sebastian Bach, who included loures in his French Suite No. 5 and Partita No. 3 for violin; André Campra; Telemann; and Christoph Graupner.
The loure is a French dance with variants in German Baroque music and dance traditions.
The loure evolved from a French folk dance linked to the Norman bagpipe tradition into a Baroque theatrical dance form.
